theme: Wisdom and rulers; death levels all; folly’s cost
readingInstruction: Read Ecclesiastes 8:1-10:20. The Preacher considers the injustice of life, the fate of death that comes to all, and the limits of human wisdom. Read with patience. These are some of the book’s hardest passages.
settingTheScene: The Preacher continues his reflection with an eye on rulers and justice. He sees that the wicked sometimes prosper and the righteous suffer, that death comes to everyone, and that wisdom does not always bring rewards. At the same time, he repeatedly calls the reader to enjoy life as a gift. These chapters are among the most puzzling and most honest in the Bible.
observation: “Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God” (8:12).
“There is a vanity that takes place on earth, that there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked” (8:14).
“It is the same for all, since the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked” (9:2).
“A living dog is better than a dead lion” (9:4).
“Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do” (9:7).
“Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going” (9:10).
“The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… but time and chance happen to them all” (9:11).
“Dead flies make the perfumer’s ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor” (10:1).
interpretation:
The Preacher is troubled by injustice. He sees wicked people buried with honor, and righteous people receiving what the wicked deserve. “There is a vanity that takes place on earth.” He does not hide it. Yet he holds fast to a central conviction: “It will be well with those who fear God.” He cannot see how, but he knows that God is just. This is faith in the dark.

Chapter 9 faces death head-on. The same fate comes to all. The living know they will die, but the dead know nothing. Our loves and hates and envies perish. This is how it looks from “under the sun,” the perspective of observation without revelation. The Preacher is describing the limits of what can be seen. He does not yet have the fullness of the resurrection hope.

Yet in the face of death, he gives a surprising command: enjoy life. “Go, eat your bread with joy.” Enjoy your wife, “all the days of your vain life.” And “whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might.” The shortness of life is not a reason for despair but for diligence and joy. Because we will not be here forever, we should live fully now and work wholeheartedly.

He also says that life is not predictable: “The race is not to the swift.” Time and chance happen to everyone. We cannot guarantee outcomes. The Preacher does not deny God’s sovereignty, but he refuses to turn the proverbs into promises. Wisdom is valuable, but no one can control how things turn out.

Chapter 10 returns to the practical, with sayings about folly and rulers. A little folly spoils much wisdom. “The words of a wise man’s mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him.” The chapter shows that wisdom matters even though it does not guarantee success.
connection: Paul says that Christ has “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10), answering the Preacher’s darkness. 1 Corinthians 15:58 says, “Your labor is not in vain in the Lord.” Jesus spoke of working “while it is day” (John 9:4). Colossians 3:23 echoes 9:10: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord.” Revelation 14:13 says the dead who die in the Lord rest from their labors and their deeds follow them.
application:
Enjoy one simple pleasure today, with thanks to God.

Do a task you have been avoiding with all your might.

If you are troubled by injustice, bring it to God, who is just even when you cannot see it.
prayerPrompts: Give God what you do not understand about life under the sun.
Ask him to teach you to enjoy his gifts with thanks and humility.
Ask him to keep you from folly’s small costs.
